title: Quantum Machine Learning for Anomaly Detection in Consumer Electronics
abstract_summary: This preprint presents a generic framework for applying quantum machine learning (QML) to anomaly detection in consumer electronics, introducing and comparing supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement QML methods (e.g., VQCs, quantum kernels, QNNs, QSVMs, quantum clustering). The authors illustrate applicability with five case studies (IoMT security, image/surveillance anomaly detection, sensor intrusion, and credit card fraud), report promising results for hybrid quantum-classical approaches, and discuss practical limitations such as limited qubit counts, noise, and the need for dimensionality reduction.
methodology_description: This paper is a systematic survey/review that (1) proposes a generic workflow for applying quantum machine learning (QML) to anomaly detection with classical data and (2) reviews and synthesizes recent QML methods and case studies in consumer-electronics-related anomaly detection. The generic workflow described comprises: preprocessing/cleaning classical data and applying dimensionality reduction (PCA, LDA, t-SNE) to fit near-term quantum resources; encoding reduced classical features into quantum states (angle encoding is emphasized); processing via parameterized quantum circuits (PQC/Ansatz) or quantum-kernel mappings to higher-dimensional Hilbert spaces; measuring expectation values or parity outputs and performing classical post-processing; and classical optimization of trainable parameters using gradient-based schemes (including the parameter-shift rule). The survey organizes QML algorithms into variational approaches (VQC/QNN/HQCNN), kernel approaches (quantum kernels / QSVM / IQP-based kernels), unsupervised quantum methods (quantum clustering via swap-test, quantum ensemble/bagging), and quantum reinforcement learning (QRL) approaches. To illustrate the methodology in practice, the authors summarize five recent empirical case studies spanning IoMT security (fused Q-DNN and QRL), hybrid quantum-classical deep anomaly detection (QHDNN replacing FC layers with VQCs), hybrid autoencoders with PQC latent processing (HAE), quantum convolutional neural networks (QCNN) for surveillance video anomaly detection, and an IQP-based quantum kernel one-class SVM for credit card fraud. The paper also discusses practical constraints observed across studies (limited qubit counts, need for dimensionality reduction and subsampling, use of hybrid classical–quantum pipelines) and reports the common experimental components (hardware or simulators used in referenced works) and evaluation metrics reported in those studies.

[supported] Hybrid quantum-classical architectures (classical preprocessing or feature reduction + parameterized quantum circuits) are the dominant practical approach in recent studies due to limited qubit counts and were used in the presented case studies.

results_summary: The preprint surveys QML approaches applied to anomaly detection in consumer-electronics-related domains and presents a general workflow (classical preprocessing → quantum encoding → variational or kernel-based quantum processing → classical optimization). Multiple case studies are summarized: hybrid QML models (quantum layers replacing or augmenting dense layers) and quantum-kernel SVM variants are shown to achieve competitive or improved anomaly detection metrics on small-scale datasets (IoMT security, MNIST/Fashion-MNIST AD, power-plant sensors, surveillance video, and a credit-card fraud dataset). The authors emphasize that most successful demonstrations are hybrid and small-scale (often run on simulators or few-qubit devices), list practical limitations (qubit count, noise, dimensionality constraints, kernel evaluation costs), and frame widespread industrial deployment as contingent on improved hardware and error correction.
performance_claims: Rajawat et al. (IoMT fused Q-DNN semisupervised): reported accuracies ranging from 92.23% to 99.34%.
Wang et al. (QHDNN for deep image anomaly detection): reported AUC = 89.41% (Fashion-MNIST best) and AUC = 88.24% (MNIST).
Sakhnenko et al. (Hybrid Autoencoder + PQC on gas turbine data): recall = 64.1% (on gas turbine test set); other datasets: Musk 100%, Arrhythmia 72.7%, Satlog 76% (benchmarks reported).
Javaria et al. (QCNN on surveillance): reported classification accuracies up to 1.00 (100%) on some scenarios and improvements over classical DCNN (e.g., 0.98 vs. 0.97 for robbery/normal).

Kyriienko & Magnusson (quantum-kernel fraud detection): reported that the quantum kernel-based classifier outperformed the classical kernel by ~15% in average precision; table reports Average Precision: ~70% (context: credit-card fraud dataset).
Authors note IQP circuit with data re-uploaded 3 times was used to increase expressivity in the credit-card study (part of the performance/implementation details).
quantum_advantage_detail: The preprint reports small-scale empirical improvements in select case studies (mostly hybrid models, simulators and few-qubit experiments) but does not demonstrate a provable, scalable quantum advantage. Claims of faster kernel evaluation or resource advantages are primarily theoretical or limited to niche experimental settings; broad, production-level advantage is presented as contingent on future fault-tolerant hardware and error correction.
limitations: Limited number of usable qubits in current quantum machines, forcing dimensionality reduction or severe feature compression before quantum processing.
Near-term quantum devices are noisy and less reliable; decoherence causes errors that limit practical performance.
Need for quantum error correction and fault-tolerant quantum computers before industrial-scale QML deployment is feasible.
Quantum circuits and QML models cannot handle large volumes of data directly — subsampling is commonly used in experiments.

Kernel-based quantum methods have significant time/space complexity for large datasets (Gram matrix construction O(N_s^2), re-evaluation O(N_s) per new data point, inference cost O(N_d N_s)), limiting real-time or mass-evaluation use-cases.
Ideal design of variational circuit (Ansatz) is an open problem; expressivity and circuit architecture choices significantly affect performance.
Training VQCs requires many repeated quantum measurements and classical optimization steps, which increases measurement overhead and training cost.
Many reported experiments rely on small datasets, heavy dimensionality reduction, low qubit counts (e.g., 4 qubits), or simulators, limiting generalizability to real-world, large-scale applications.
[inferred] Quantum advantage claims are currently demonstrated in constrained settings; it is unclear how these advantages scale to production workloads.
[inferred] Selecting and validating quantum encoding/feature-mapping strategies for complex classical data remains challenging and ill-specified for many anomaly detection tasks.
[inferred] Risk of overfitting or poor generalization when using hybrid/small-quantum models on skewed or limited anomaly datasets.
[inferred] Measurement shot noise, optimizer stability, and barren-plateau-like optimization issues may restrict reliable training of PQCs on NISQ hardware.

contradictions: The paper reports claimed empirical advantages of QML on small benchmark datasets (e.g., Rajawat et al., Wang et al.) but simultaneously emphasizes that most demonstrations are simulator-only or few-qubit and require heavy dimensionality reduction — raising a contradiction between reported quantum superiority and limited real-world applicability.

Authors present strong future-oriented claims (industrial savings, 'light and flexible' models) while acknowledging lack of production-scale demonstrations and substantial hardware limitations (qubit counts, noise), contradicting the strength of some advantage claims.

Performance improvements reported for quantum-kernel and hybrid QML methods on small datasets contradict broad scalability claims: improvements do not necessarily generalize to large, high-dimensional financial datasets without advances in qubit counts and error correction.
